logline: An arrogant department store CEO and a tough, penniless stuntwoman find themselves inexplicably swapping bodies, forcing each to inhabit the other's world and, grudgingly, feelings.

renewal.note: Single-season fantasy romance completed January 16, 2011. No sequel produced. The series remains a foundational K-drama in the body-swap romance subgenre and is consistently listed on classic K-drama recommendation lists.

bollymeter.basis: Hyun Bin's comedic performance during the body-swap sections earned near-universal praise and cemented his leading-man status; the romantic tension holds, though Ra-im's character gets underwritten relative to Joo-won.

pull_quotes.text: This was the most addictive K-drama for me since Boys Over Flowers.
Secret Garden is one of those dramas that gets better as it progresses.

seasons.review_body: Secret Garden premiered November 13, 2010 on SBS and ran 20 episodes through January 2011, with strong national ratings that showcased Hyun Bin's range in balancing comedy and dramatic weight. The body-swap sequences stand out, with a CEO inhabiting a stuntwoman's physicality and social register through sustained comic invention that rarely comes from a leading male in the genre. The show’s central weakness also stands out: Gil Ra-im is comparatively underwritten, and the writing channels creativity into Joo-won at Ra-im's expense. The ending lands with qualified payoff, and the series endures as a genre touchstone for body-swap romance, continuing to surface on classic K-drama recommendation lists more than a decade on.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body: Secret Garden Season 1 Episode 1 aired November 13, 2010 on SBS as the premiere of the 20-episode series. IMDb audience scored the season 8.0. Nose in a Book called it the most addictive K-drama since Boys Over Flowers. The premiere engineers the collision between the glittering CEO world and the stunt unit - two social registers whose incompatibility the show treats as both comic engine and romantic obstacle. Hyun Bin's Joo-won is rendered immediately and broadly: the aristocratic contempt is performed without apology. Ra-im's capability in physical work is established alongside her class positioning, giving the body-swap premise an emotional logic before the supernatural element arrives. The episode's closing ambiguity signals that the tonal register will allow both humour and consequence.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere engineers the collision between the world of Korean celebrity and the action-film stunt unit, establishing the class gulf that the series will use as both comic engine and emotional obstacle. Hyun Bin's arrogant CEO is rendered immediately and broadly, though already with hints of the comedic range the show will later exploit.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Joo-won's first dismissal of Ra-im - the aristocratic contempt that sets the push-pull tension for the entire run.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 20
episode_reviews.review_body: Secret Garden Season 1 Episode 20 aired January 16, 2011 on SBS as the finale of the 20-episode series. IMDb audience scored the season 8.0. Jae-Ha Kim noted the show 'gets better as it progresses.' The finale resolves the supernatural premise and the class-divide romance by steering away from the pure fantasy conclusion the genre typically provides. For viewers who invested in the body-swap's comedic and emotional possibilities, the ending functions as a genuine landing; for those expecting genre conventions to hold completely, it reads as a partial disappointment. Hyun Bin's comedic work across the body-swap sequences had been the season's most discussed performance element, and the finale closes that arc with appropriate weight.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale resolves the supernatural premise and the class-divide romance with a strong dose of reality, steering away from the pure fantasy conclusion the genre usually delivers. The ending lands as earned for some while feeling anticlimactic for others.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final body-swap resolution scene, where the show commits to the emotional consequences its premise set up.
